item.title: [9] Beyond Best-of-$k$: Prior-Consistent DAPS for Ambiguous Nonlinear Inverse Problems
item.description:
Score 9/10 · arXiv

Prior-consistent DAPS directly tackles your core problem of diffusion posterior sampling for ambiguous nonlinear inverse problems like phase retrieval (the crystallographic phase problem), and exposes how best-of-k evaluation hides prior-inconsistent solutions.

Merve Kocabas, Benjamin A. Burns, Andreas Geiger, Kent Gauen, Sara Fridovich-Keil

arXiv:2610.31592v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diffusion models have become strong priors for solving inverse problems. However, nonlinear inverse problems such as phase retrieval remain challenging when multiple measurement-consistent solutions are distinguishable only by the prior; we call such measurements ambiguous. Existing diffusion-based samplers rely on local approximations during reconstruction. For an ambiguous measurement, these approximations can allow measurement guidance to favor a measurement-consistent mode that is close to a prior-supported mode but is itself not supported by the prior. Evaluation often masks this type of failure by reporting the best-of-$k$ runs, where the best is selected by comparison to the ground truth. We introduce Prior-Consistent DAPS (PC-DAPS), a variant of Decoupled Annealing Posterior Sampling (DAPS) designed to address this failure case by maintaining multiple candidate solutions within a single sampling run. As annealing noise decreases, PC-DAPS prunes and replaces weaker candidates according to their prior consistency, without any ground-truth access. PC-DAPS reduces the incidence of prior-inconsistent samples and improves sample quality on nonlinear inverse problems while preserving sample quality and diversity on linear inverse problems.

item.title: [7] MutaStruct: Revisiting Benchmarks for Single-Site Mutation-Induced Structural Change Prediction
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

MutaStruct shows that a Copy-WT control stays competitive on backbone metrics while rankings shift on mutation-site metrics, which is a pointed critique of whether structure predictors capture mutation-induced conformational change rather than memorizing the wild type.

Huynh, T.-P., Ho, D.-M., Nguyen, V. T. D., Kha, Q.-H. et al.

Predicting the structural consequences of single-site mutations is fundamental to understanding protein function, disease mechanisms, and protein engineering. However, existing benchmarks for mutation-induced structural change prediction are often affected by duplicate mutation events, highly similar structural pairs, and experimental-state confounders, which can inflate reported performance. We introduce MutaStruct, a curated benchmark of experimentally observed single-mutation protein structure pairs designed for rigorous evaluation of mutation-induced structural changes. MutaStruct combines residue-level sequence validation, coordinate-level quality control, context-aware filtering, event-level deduplication, and leakage-aware data splitting to improve dataset reliability and evaluation rigor. We benchmark sequence-only structure prediction, physics-based refinement, and learning-based refinement methods together with a Copy-WT diagnostic control. Copy-WT remains highly competitive on backbone-based metrics, while method rankings change substantially across local and mutation-site measures. These results show that overall structural fidelity does not necessarily imply accurate modeling of mutation-associated structural change, underscoring the need for further methodological development beyond current paradigms. The benchmark dataset is currently undergoing further curation and expansion and will be released in a future journal-version update. The codebase, trained models, and evaluation pipeline are publicly available at https://github.com/HySonLab/MutaStruct

item.title: [9] QUBO-Based Conformer Selection with Quantum-Classical Hybrid Optimization for Multiconformer Ligand Modeling
item.description:
Score 9/10 · arXiv

Directly reformulates qFit-ligand multiconformer selection as a QUBO and benchmarks it against the MIQP baseline on 83 X-ray ligand entries using composite-omit map RSCC and EDIAm, including the notable finding that map agreement and atom-level density support diverge.

Jiyun Lee, Haeseong Kim, Junho Lee, Joonsuk Huh

arXiv:2610.29058v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A ligand can adopt multiple conformations within the same binding site, and these conformations can interact differently with the surrounding protein. Multiconformer modeling must therefore determine which candidate conformations to retain and what occupancies to assign to them. An established automated approach uses mixed-integer quadratic programming (MIQP) with hard occupancy and conformer-count limits for this selection. Here, we reformulated conformer selection as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem with finite penalties and discrete occupancies. We solved the QUBO using a quantum-classical hybrid solver. We compared this workflow with the MIQP-based qFit-ligand workflow across 83 paired X-ray ligand entries using the same experimental inputs and the same qFit-ligand processing protocol. For each entry, both final models were evaluated against the same composite-omit map generated from the common input structure before the two workflows diverged. Quantum-qFit produced higher ligand-region real-space correlation coefficients (RSCC) in 62 entries 74.7% and lower occupancy-weighted torsional strain in 66 entries 79.5%. Similar directional trends remained in the 28 entries with matched final conformer counts. The molecular Electron Density for Individual Atoms score (EDIAm) decreased in most entries. This result shows that higher regional map agreement did not necessarily correspond to stronger atom-level density support. Overall, the results show that the conformer-selection formulation can change which ligand states are represented from the same experimental data and provide a QUBO framework for studying multiconformer ligand selection.

item.title: [8] Internal Guidance as a Sampling Method for Tilted Diffusion Models
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Proposes a new training-free route to reward-tilted diffusion sampling by evaluating the base denoiser at shifted, rescaled inputs rather than adding drift terms, which is a genuinely new guidance idea even though it is shown on discrete hypercube data.

Curtis McDonald, Peter Bartlett

arXiv:2610.29086v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reward guidance methods sample an exponential tilt of a base density using a diffusion model trained with only samples from the base distribution. Existing methods use what we call external guidance: additive terms in the drift or multiplicative terms on the transition probabilities. We propose internal guidance which leaves the output of the base denoiser unmodified and instead changes the point at which it is evaluated. For discrete distributions embedded in the hypercube $\{-1,1\}^{d}$, the denoiser of any linearly tilted density is exactly the base denoiser evaluated at a shifted and rescaled input. In practice the base denoiser is a neural network trained on noised samples of the base distribution. The required evaluation points for sampling the tilted density would be out-of-distribution for basic noising of the base distribution. We modify the training algorithm with random diagonal rescalings of the data, so that the denoiser network learns both in- and out-of-distribution evaluations of the denoiser relative to the base distribution. A single denoiser network samples binary reward tilts, class labels, and infilling with no fine-tuning and no external guidance term.

item.title: [8] DEEP: Extracting Latent Energetic Landscapes from Protein Structure Predictors
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

DEEP extracts statistical potentials from Boltz-2's own distograms and shows these cofolding models encode energetic information that AlphaFold2 lacks, bearing directly on what Boltz learns versus memorizes and on using it as a prior for conformations.

Rozsa, Z. B., Erdos, G.

Modern protein structure predictors learn complex sequence-structure relationships, yet the extent to which their internal representations capture the energetic principles governing protein stability and conformational preferences remains unclear. Here, we introduce DEEP (Distogram Encoded Energetic Potential), a general framework that extracts effective statistical potentials directly from predicted residue-pair distance distributions, using the models own terminal distance state as an internal reference without training on experimental stability data. Applied to Boltz-2 (DEEP-Boltz) achieves a mean per-assay Spearman correlation of 0.720 across 64 ProteinGym stability assays, numerically outperforming all 97 published zero-shot methods in the matched comparison on level with the best performing predictors trained directly on experimental stability measurements. Beyond mutation effects, DEEP-Boltz accurately distinguishes native-like from non-native conformations across more than 180,000 Rosetta decoys. Applying DEEP to AlphaFold2 reveals nearly identical conformational discrimination but substantially weaker mutation-effect prediction, demonstrating that recognizing favorable conformations and capturing their energetic sensitivity to sequence changes are distinct properties of learned structural representations. Together, these findings establish that protein structure predictors encode accessible energetic information beyond their geometric predictions and that this information can be extracted. We release the framework and DEEP-Boltz as a freely available tool for extracting these latent energetic representations and for zero-shot prediction of mutation-induced protein stability changes.

item.title: [7] Compositional neural networks for multimodal X-ray and neutron scattering inversion
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Single-observation flow-matching posterior estimators combined only at inference time to co-refine X-ray and neutron data is a direct template for fusing multiple experimental restraints in a generative prior, though applied to thin-film reflectometry rather than biomolecules.

Valentin Munteanu, Alexander Hinderhofer, Dmitry Lapkin, Vladimir Starostin, Frank Schreiber

arXiv:2610.29362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: X-ray and neutron scattering are indispensable for structural characterization across condensed-matter physics and materials science. Yet, because scattering experiments generally record intensities without phase information, distinct structures can yield similar scattering patterns, rendering the corresponding inverse problems non-unique. This ambiguity can be reduced by combining complementary measurements, but their integration into machine-learning frameworks remains challenging. Here we introduce a modular framework for probabilistic multi-measurement analysis based on prior-amortized flow matching. Single-observation posterior estimators are trained separately for individual observation types or physical probes and combined only at inference time through a compositional sampler. This late fusion approach allows pretrained single-observation models to be reused without dedicated joint retraining. As a case in point, we consider reflectometry, which provides depth-resolved, nanometer-scale information about thin films and interfaces. Our single-observation demonstrations span X-ray, time-of-flight neutron and polarized neutron reflectometry. In separate co-refinement studies, task-matched estimators enable homogeneous composition across multiple neutron contrasts and heterogeneous multimodal composition of X-ray and neutron measurements. Together, these results establish compositional flow matching as a modular approach to uncertainty-aware inversion and co-refinement, with potential applicability to other scattering problems in which multiple observations constrain a common physical structure while retaining measurement-specific parameters.

item.title: [7] Multi-Objective Protein Optimization via Modular Diffusion Steering
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Modular inference-time diffusion steering with scalar rewards that can be paired with different diffusion models and steering procedures closely mirrors the plug-in guidance architecture of your sampleworks platform, applied to protein optimization, though it builds on existing steering methods.

Meir Roketlishvili, Felix Huber, Wenda Chu, Yisong Yue, Raul Astudillo

arXiv:2610.28943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protein engineering often requires improving several properties simultaneously, motivating the search for high-performing sequences that represent useful fitness tradeoffs. Discovering these sequences is challenging because the design space is combinatorially large and experimental campaigns often permit only a few rounds of batched measurements. We introduce \textit{MODS}, a modular framework for multi-objective protein optimization via inference-time diffusion steering. For each proposal, MODS samples augmented Chebyshev scalarization weights and a fitness-surrogate ensemble member to define a scalar steering reward. Varying the weights directs generation toward different objective tradeoffs, while varying ensemble members diversifies the predictions used for guidance. Because MODS expresses multi-objective acquisition through scalar rewards, it can be paired with different diffusion models and compatible steering procedures. After each evaluation batch, MODS updates the surrogates without retraining the generative model. We evaluate MODS on six protein optimization tasks using predictive oracles trained on experimental assay data, with two diffusion models and two steering procedures. MODS achieves competitive final hypervolume across all six tasks with both diffusion models, and substantially outperforms the best evaluated baseline on several tasks. Our results demonstrate a flexible and effective approach to multi-objective protein optimization with limited feedback.

item.title: [8] Hilbert-Scale Stability of Posterior Diffusion Priors for Ill-Posed Signal Recovery
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Non-asymptotic stability theory for posterior diffusion on ill-posed linear inverse problems, including a result that operator-adapted posterior correction beats isotropic guidance, is directly relevant to steering diffusion priors with experimental data.

Bahman Moraffah, Raha Moraffah

arXiv:2610.27030v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Indirect and noisy observations are difficult to invert when the forward operator smooths out the unknown signal. In this case, the unstable modes are precisely the modes that the data reveals least, thus the success of any reconstruction method depends on how prior information interacts with the geometry of the operator across regularity scales. Diffusion priors have become ubiquitous for such problems; however, the current theory still does not determine when a learned score remains informative under ill-posed forward operators. In this paper, we study posterior diffusion for linear inverse problems on Hilbert scales and derive a stability theory under an explicit score-amplification condition. Under a smoothing condition on the forward map, a source condition on the truth, and weak-norm control of score error, we derive non-asymptotic recovery bounds in \(\Hs^s\) that separate observation noise, score approximation, and reverse-time discretization. These bounds give a recoverable regularity threshold determined jointly by operator smoothing, truth regularity, score regularity, and the posterior correction. The threshold specifies the Hilbert-scale norms \(\Hs^s\) in which weak-norm score error remains controlled after propagation through the posterior reverse dynamics. For larger regularity indices \(s\), the inverse geometry magnifies the same error, and the Hilbert-scale recovery estimate no longer gives uniform stability. We also prove that a posterior correction adapted to the forward operator improves stability relative to isotropic guidance in the regularity ranges where the smoothing action of the forward map matters most. The recovery estimates give a regularity-sensitive theory of posterior diffusion and show how learned score error, operator smoothing, and reconstruction norm jointly determine the stable range predicted by the analysis.

item.title: [8] Reliable and Efficient Agentic Protein Design with Toolset Harnessing
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

Baker lab's Chaperone harness wires RFdiffusion3, AF3 and 50+ tools into an agent-friendly design workflow and reports an 86% token reduction with a real cortisol-binder campaign, directly on your agents-for-structural-biology interest.

Butcher, J., Chen, J., Hunt, A., Haas, C. M. et al.

Computational protein design workflows require the orchestration of multiple tools, data formats, and analysis steps that are often fragmented. Here, we introduce Chaperone, a lightweight and customizable framework that enables seamless integration of RFdiffusion3 (RFD3) with downstream sequence design, structure prediction, and evaluation tools, including ProteinMPNN, AlphaFold3 (AF3), and more than 50 other protein design tools. By combining a programmable agent-friendly interface with parallelized execution on high-performance computing systems, Chaperone as a harness enables rapid iteration and scalable exploration of complex protein design workflows. Across an evaluation of nine biomolecular design tasks, we find using Chaperone reduces total token usage relative to baseline agents by 86% and GPU costs by 64%, while increasing the overall computational design pass rate. We demonstrate Chaperones utility for large-scale design-space exploration through a two-week end-to-end small-molecule binder design campaign, yielding low nanomolar binders to cortisol zero shot. We further demonstrate its versatility across distinct design challenges, including the design of a symmetric 12-subunit self-assembly nanoparticle and a linker that mediates interactions between C2- and D3-symmetric protein complexes to form crystalline assemblies. Together, these results demonstrate how agent harnesses built around standardized tool interfaces can substantially improve the efficiency and success of complex, long-horizon agentic design workflows in biology. We make Chaperone freely available to the community on GitHub: https://github.com/RosettaCommons/chaperone.

item.title: [7] Large Deviations in Stochastic Dynamics: A Hamiltonian Perspective
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Lecture notes from Vanden-Eijnden and Rotskoff on large deviations, quasipotentials and metastability give a unified treatment of the SDE and transition-rate mathematics behind ensemble sampling.

Lorenzo Cirigliano, William D. Pi\~{n}eros, Anna Poggialini, Grant M. Rotskoff, Eric Vanden-Eijnden

arXiv:2610.27179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: These lecture notes present an introduction to large deviations in stochastic dynamical systems, adapted from a lecture series given at the Les Houches school ``Large Deviations: Theory and Applications'' in July 2024. The exposition develops the theory through a unified methodology: WKB analysis of backward Kolmogorov equations, which reveals the Hamiltonian structure underlying all large deviation principles considered here. We treat three asymptotic regimes systematically. First, the small-noise limit for stochastic differential equations and the large-volume limit for Markov jump processes, where the Large Deviation Principle emerges from the Law of Large Numbers through progressively finer characterizations of fluctuations. Second, the long-time limit combined with small noise, yielding the quasipotential formalism for metastability and transition rates in both equilibrium and nonequlibrium systems. Third, the long-time limit at finite noise, connecting to spectral methods via tilted generators and enabling reduction of multiscale systems.We survey computational approaches including minimum action methods, their geometric variants for quasipotential calculations, and neural network techniques. The Schl\"{o}gl model of chemical bistability serves as a running example, illustrating both scalar and spatially extended settings. Appendices provide self-contained background on stochastic calculus and Markov jump processes.

item.title: [7] Variable-Resolution Scattering Reveals Ensemble Properties
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

TENOR-SAXS recovers the width of the Rg distribution, not just its mean, from a single 2D scattering image, which bears directly on how SAXS restraints for conformational ensembles should be interpreted.

Uri Steinitz, Mathar Kravikass, Gil Koren, Roy Beck

arXiv:2610.28215v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: SAXS/SANS determine the size and structure of particles and macromolecules in solution. However, the conventional low-angle determination of the radius of gyration, Rg, cannot separately resolve its scattering-weighted mean and the width of its distribution. Because the apparent Rg includes a contribution from ensemble variance, the distribution width is required even to recover the mean Rg. Here, we introduce TENOR-SAXS, a method for estimating the scattering-weighted width of an Rg distribution by applying two anisotropic digital smearings to a single 2D scattering image. Comparing the smeared images provides curvature information unavailable from the conventional radial profile. The resulting observables require no explicit model of the native instrumental point-spread function and show only weak sensitivity over the range of native resolutions typical of SAXS measurements examined here. Analytical expressions are derived in the low-angle and narrow-distribution limits for ensembles described by a known or independently constrained single-particle form factor. For verification, we simulated scattering by particles with several form factors and ensembles with different size distributions, all agree well with the analytical theory. To leading order, the principal observable depends on the scattering-weighted mean and variance rather than on the distribution's functional form or higher moments. For simulated data corresponding to feasible synchrotron exposure times for biological samples, the distribution width and, expressed as a fraction of its mean, was recovered with a typical discrepancy of ~0.1, while the scattering-weighted mean Rg was recovered with ~2% relative discrepancy. TENOR-SAXS thus provides a framework for estimating ensemble width from existing 2D scattering data without explicit instrumental desmearing and for correcting the variance contribution to the apparent radius

item.title: [7] Diffractograph: single-particle reconstruction using electron-diffraction data
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

Diffractograph reconstructs 3D structure from single-particle electron diffraction, using a cryo-EM map for low-resolution phases and density modification for extension, which echoes crystallography-style phasing and is a new route to structure determination you likely haven't seen.

Matinyan, S., Abrahams, J. P.

We recently showed that narrow-beam electron diffraction of single particles provides higher signal-to-noise ratios and lower radiation damage than imaging. Here we introduce Diffractograph, a suite for reconstructing three-dimensional structure from these data. Diffractograph selects mutually compatible diffraction frames, groups them into one or more models and discards incompatible frames. In the ab initio workflow, this is done without prior structural information. In the reference-guided workflow, a low-resolution electrostatic potential map from single-particle cryo-EM is used to select compatible frames and determine their orientations. The oriented frames are combined into a three-dimensional intensity distribution. The reference map supplies low-resolution phases for the oversampled structure factors, and density modification extends these phases to higher resolution. For synthetic 200-keV diffraction data extending to 2.2 A, Diffractograph retained all frames and recovered the correct orientation of every retained frame with a median plane-normal error of 0.27 degrees. These results establish a computational workflow for structure determination using single-particle electron-diffraction data.

item.title: [9] REFLEX: RNA Ensemble Generation via Flexibility-Calibrated Stochastic Bridge
item.description:
Score 9/10 · arXiv

REFLEX generates multi-conformer RNA ensembles with an SE(3) stochastic bridge calibrated by experimental B-factors and evaluates coverage against experimentally observed states, squarely in your conformational-ensemble and data-informed generative modeling territory.

Wanli Ma, Tianmeng Hu, Ke Li

arXiv:2610.26261v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: RNA molecules often function through multiple experimentally observed conformational states. A central challenge is to capture ensemble diversity without sacrificing structural fidelity: samples may collapse toward averaged representative structures or drift into unsupported conformational regions. We introduce REFLEX (RNA Ensemble generation calibrated by FLEXibility), a sequence-conditioned generator for RNA backbone-frame ensembles based on a heteroscedastic stochastic bridge on SE(3). During training, experimental B-factors calibrate residue-wise bridge widths, exposing each observed conformer through local perturbation neighborhoods with residue-specific scales while keeping constrained regions sharper. A learned flexibility condition guides the bridge-field network to recover target conformer-specific frames from these calibrated noisy states. At inference, REFLEX uses only the input sequence, requiring no MSA-subsampling heuristics. On a multi-conformer RNA benchmark, REFLEX achieves the best precision-recall trade-off for ensemble coverage across evaluation thresholds, while recovery-stress ablations indicate gains in target-frame recovery under stronger perturbations.

item.title: [9] Steered Not Stirred: Effective Reward Tilting using Surrogate Reward Mixing
item.description:
Score 9/10 · arXiv

MARTINI composes cheap surrogate rewards to steer pretrained diffusion and flow models toward an unavailable experimental oracle at inference time, and reports gains in protein-ligand cofolding pose accuracy, so it speaks directly to your steering-with-experimental-data setting.

Alec Sargood, Olivia Gallup, Georg Maierhofer, Noam Ghenassia, Paul Duckworth, Krisztina Sinkovics, Avishek Joey Bose

arXiv:2610.25502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous-time generative models, from diffusion models, flow matching, and now flow maps, owe their practical value to high-fidelity generation and steerability. In many applications, a ground-truth latent ``oracle'' reward $R^*$ is unavailable or expensive to evaluate, e.g., human judgments or experimental measurements. Although the oracle reward is not directly observable, it can often be approximated through multiple cheaper surrogates that, individually, provide incomplete characterizations but collectively reveal substantial information about the downstream task. In this paper, we present a method for composing such surrogates to steer a pretrained model toward the distribution tilted by an unavailable $R^*$. Given a small feedback set of oracle rankings or numerical rewards, we introduce Mixing And Reward Tilting for INference-time Improvement (MARTINI), which learns a surrogate composition for plug-and-play use with standard inference-time steering methods. Our theory characterizes surrogate information limits and relates population recovery error to ideal-target KL at small tilt strength. For preferences, the bound additionally accounts for an irreducible mismatch between the Plackett-Luce population target and the conditional mean. Experiments demonstrate improved oracle-tilt fidelity in language generation and ImageNet alignment, and improved joint pose accuracy and validity in protein-ligand cofolding, without inference-time oracle queries.

item.title: [8] Gradient-Free Noise Optimization for Reward Alignment in Generative Models
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

ZeNO is a gradient-free, path-integral noise-optimization method for inference-time reward steering of diffusion and flow models that explicitly handles a protein structure generation task where backprop is infeasible, directly relevant to steering Boltz-style models with non-differentiable experimental scores.

Jeongsol Kim, Hongeun Kim, Jian Wang, Jong Chul Ye

arXiv:2605.11347v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing reward alignment methods for diffusion and flow models rely on multi-step stochastic trajectories, making them difficult to extend to deterministic generators. A natural alternative is noise-space optimization, but existing approaches require backpropagation through the generator and reward pipeline, limiting applicability to differentiable settings. To address this, here we present ZeNO (Zeroth-order Noise Optimization), a gradient-free framework that formulates noise optimization as a path-integral control problem, estimable from zeroth-order reward evaluations. When instantiated with an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck reference process and a one-step receding horizon, the repeated update connects to Langevin dynamics targeting a reward-tilted distribution. ZeNO enables effective inference-time scaling and demonstrates strong performance across diverse generators and reward functions, including a protein structure generation task where backpropagation is infeasible.

item.title: [8] PnP-CF: A Consensus Flow-Matching Solver for General Inverse Problems
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

A flow-matching plug-and-play solver with ADMM-style consensus that extends to nonlinear forward operators, including learned neural ones, is directly relevant to using generative priors for inverse problems such as map or density fitting.

Dibyanshu Kumar, Magda Gregorova

arXiv:2610.26000v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Plug-and-Play (PnP) methods using continuous-time deep generative models as learned data distribution priors enable synthesizing high-quality solutions of model-based inverse problems. The quality of the solutions depends critically on the interplay and consensus between the inverse problem solver and the generative model sampler. We revisit a recently introduced flow-based PnP framework, which we refer to as PnP-CF (Consensus Flow), and extend its application to nonlinear inverse problems, including those with learned neural-network forward operators. PnP-CF combines a flow-matching denoiser with (i) ADMM-like dual variable updates and (ii) a time-adaptive pullback onto the intermediate flow probability path that combines a stochastic and a deterministic component. We discuss how these two features stabilize the algorithm and promote consensus, and demonstrate on a set of experiments that PnP-CF not only solves standard linear inverse problems with quality at least comparable to state-of-the-art baselines, but also extends gracefully to nonlinear inverse problems, including forward operators realized by pretrained neural networks, for which existing methods produce unsatisfactory results or fail completely.

item.title: [8] ProteinGeoBench: Frontier Structural-Biology Agents Are Fluent at Lookup but Lost in Geometry
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

A statistically careful benchmark of frontier agents on 131 protein-structure tasks, showing they look up metadata well but compute geometry poorly, is directly the agent-for-structural-biology evaluation you would want to know about.

Matt Turk, Brandon L. Neel, Diana M. Lopez, Zachary D. Smith, Grace N. Johnecheck, James B. Golden

arXiv:2610.26829v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Frontier agents retrieve structural metadata well and compute geometry from coordinates less reliably. We ask how much of a benchmark score reflects that gap and how much reflects the evaluation configuration around the model. We study ProteinGeoBench, a suite of 131 protein-structure tasks, using 4,249 rollouts from four frontier models and 4,486 further trials across 26 models. Three of the four frontier models fall within 0.031 of one another (0.785 to 0.816) with no difference between them resolved, while the fourth scores 0.707 and all three gaps to it exclude zero. Three of the four do better on metadata lookup than on numeric calculation. The fourth is slightly better on numeric. Numeric tasks are 28 of the 131 but half of the twelve tasks that all four models fail. The ranking also depends on the evaluation budget: with one run per task, 23.9% of bootstrap replicates put a different model first. On a selected 15-task slice, removing network access lowers scores more than blocking eight structural-database domains, but the two contrasts were graded in different passes and cannot be cleanly decomposed. Swapping in each model's own command-line agent changes scores by -0.071 to +0.086, a comparison too small to rule out moderate harness effects. Across 26 models, numeric performance rises with non-numeric performance rather than staying flat. The experiments use different task subsets, so they cannot rank model, harness, access and task composition against one another. Evaluations should report results by task family, along with the number of runs, the harness and the access conditions.

item.title: [8] Solving Inverse Problems via Diffusion-Based Priors: An Approximation-Free Ensemble Sampling Approach
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

This approximation-free ensemble SMC method for posterior sampling with pretrained diffusion priors on inverse problems, with error bounds in terms of score error and particle count, is closely aligned with steering diffusion models by experimental data, though demonstrated on imaging.

Haoxuan Chen, Yinuo Ren, Martin Renqiang Min, Lexing Ying, Zachary Izzo

arXiv:2506.03979v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have proven to be effective in modeling high-dimensional distributions, leading to their widespread adoption for representing complex priors in Bayesian inverse problems (BIPs). However, current DM-based posterior sampling methods proposed for solving common BIPs rely on heuristic approximations to the generative process. To exploit the generative capability of DMs and avoid the usage of such approximations, we propose an ensemble-based algorithm that performs posterior sampling without the use of heuristic approximations. Our algorithm is motivated by existing work that combines DM-based methods with the sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) method. By examining how the prior evolves through the diffusion process encoded by the pre-trained score function, we derive a modified partial differential equation (PDE) governing the evolution of the corresponding posterior distribution. This PDE includes a modified diffusion term and a reweighting term, which can be simulated via stochastic weighted particle methods. Theoretically, we prove that the error between the true posterior and the empirical distribution of the generated samples can be bounded in terms of the training error of the pre-trained score function and the number of particles in the ensemble. Empirically, we validate our algorithm on several inverse problems in imaging to show that our method gives more accurate reconstructions compared to existing DM-based methods. Our code is available at the following Github repository~\url{https://github.com/HaoxuanSteveC00/AFDPS-TMLR}.

item.title: [7] DiMOS: Doob-Guided Inference-Time Multi-Objective Search for Scientific Design
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

DiMOS offers gradient-free, Doob-guided local resampling with trajectory search for training-free multi-objective guidance of frozen masked diffusion models on protein and RNA tasks, close to your inference-time steering interests, though it targets sequence design and builds on established SMC-style ideas.

Ziqing Wang, Qijie Zhu, Weimin Wu, Zeqi Ye, Minshuo Chen, Han Liu, Kaize Ding

arXiv:2610.05808v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scientific design often requires jointly satisfying multiple objectives and constraints. Pretrained masked diffusion models provide a generative foundation for this task, but fine-tuning them to meet these objectives and constraints incurs additional training costs, motivating inference-time guidance with frozen models. However, such guidance faces two challenges: pass-or-fail constraints and black-box reward models may provide no useful gradients, while jointly satisfying multiple requirements can leave a small feasible region, making feasible designs difficult to find within a limited inference budget. To address these challenges, we introduce DiMOS, a training-free framework for multi-objective scientific design. Using joint rewards from candidate completions, DiMOS performs approximate Doob-guided local resampling without requiring reward gradients. To allocate computation efficiently, it uses budget-efficient trajectory search to focus computation on promising continuations. Across six DNA, protein, and RNA tasks, DiMOS attains the highest joint success rate at comparable generation times, up to $1.98\times$ the strongest baseline on DNA and protein, while maintaining high sequence uniqueness and naturalness.

item.title: [7] Rigidity-Aware Geometric Pretraining for Protein Design and Conformational Ensembles
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

RigidSSL pretrains a rigidity-aware flow-matching model on AFDB plus MD trajectories and reports more realistic GPCR conformational ensembles, which is relevant to ensemble generation, though its main emphasis is de novo design designability rather than steering with experimental data.

Zhanghan Ni, Yanjing Li, Zeju Qiu, Bernhard Sch\"olkopf, Hongyu Guo, Weiyang Liu, Shengchao Liu

arXiv:2603.02406v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative models have recently advanced $\textit{de novo}$ protein design by learning the statistical regularities of natural structures. However, current approaches face three key limitations: (1) Existing methods cannot jointly learn protein geometry and design tasks, where pretraining can be a solution; (2) Current pretraining methods mostly rely on local, non-rigid atomic representations for property prediction downstream tasks, limiting global geometric understanding for protein generation tasks; and (3) Existing approaches have yet to effectively model the rich dynamic and conformational information of protein structures. To overcome these issues, we introduce $\textbf{RigidSSL}$ ($\textit{Rigidity-Aware Self-Supervised Learning}$), a geometric pretraining framework that front-loads geometry learning prior to generative finetuning. Phase I (RigidSSL-Perturb) learns geometric priors from 432K structures from the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database with simulated perturbations. Phase II (RigidSSL-MD) refines these representations on 1.3K molecular dynamics trajectories to capture physically realistic transitions. Underpinning both phases is a bi-directional, rigidity-aware flow matching objective that jointly optimizes translational and rotational dynamics to maximize mutual information between conformations. Empirically, RigidSSL variants improve designability by up to 43% while enhancing novelty and diversity in unconditional generation. Furthermore, RigidSSL-Perturb improves the success rate by 5.8% in zero-shot motif scaffolding and RigidSSL-MD captures more biophysically realistic conformational ensembles in G protein-coupled receptor modeling.

item.title: [7] Bootstrap Stochastic Interpolant Tree for Inference-time Search Under Sparse Reward
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

A tree-based stochastic-interpolant sampler that sidesteps the per-step reward bias of SMC-style steering is a genuinely different inference-time search idea that could transfer to guided structure sampling under sparse rewards.

Binglin Ji, Anindya Sarkar, Yevgeniy Vorobeychik

arXiv:2610.24185v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tree-based samplers offer a compelling alternative for scalable inference-time search, bypassing the per-step reward and gradient dependencies that introduce systematic bias into SMC-style frameworks. Despite this advantage, contemporary tree samplers fail to achieve broad exploration. Their reliance on learned, DDPM-like transitions inherently couples neighbor states in a trajectory, thereby restricting child-parent feature divergence in the tree sampler. Consequently, these samplers suffer from restricted coverage of the target marginal distribution, severely hindering the exploration critical for efficient search under sparse reward. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a simple yet effective Bootstrap Stochastic Interpolant Tree (BSIT) sampler that decouples child node generation from explicit parent dependencies. By expanding the degrees of freedom during child node sampling, BSIT encourages diverse trajectory rollouts and unlocks broader path-space diversity-the exact catalyst needed for efficient exploration. Crucially, we show that BSIT's improved exploration accelerates convergence to the target distribution while achieving broader distributional coverage than samplers that rely on DDPM-like transitions for child-node generation, all without incurring additional function evaluations or reward feedback, thereby providing a highly efficient basis for rare target search. Extensive experiments across diverse search settings, including rare-species discovery and target-aligned molecule generation tasks, demonstrate BSIT's superior search efficiency over the baselines.

item.title: [9] Capturing α-synuclein polymorphism with AlphaFold 3 and rivals
item.description:
Score 9/10 · bioRxiv

Benchmarks AlphaFold 3, Boltz-2 and OpenFold 3 on sampling alpha-synuclein fibril polymorphs and shows template steering recovers 13 of 16 folds, a direct evaluation of cofolding models' multi-state sampling and what they over-represent.

Price, R. M., LaCourse, B., Voorspoels, A., Elliott, L. G. et al.

Amyloid fibrils formed by a single protein can adopt many distinct folds, or polymorphs, which differ between diseases and shape the surfaces available to therapeutics and diagnostics. Whether deep-learning structure prediction can capture this diversity is unclear, and the field lacks an objective definition of a polymorph from which to judge this. Here we cluster the -synuclein structures in the Protein Data Bank by TM-score, giving an objective reference set of known polymorphs. Against this reference we assess AlphaFold 3, Boltz-2 and OpenFold 3 run through ABCFold. All three produced fibril-like assemblies, though they differed in which polymorphs they reached. With templates included as default the methods over-represented the dominant fold. When untemplated the methods produced a substantial number of models matching no known structure, a subset of which have the stacking geometry of genuine fibrils. Supplying a polymorph as a template recovered 13 of 16 target folds, but only when alignment depth and the number of modelled chains were varied together. These results establish that current methods sample real -synuclein structural space and can be steered through it, and provide a framework for assessing prediction methods on amyloid targets.

item.title: [9] ConforFlux: Particle-Guided Trunk Repulsion for Diverse Protein Conformations
item.description:
Score 9/10 · bioRxiv

ConforFlux does inference-time repulsion guidance on Boltz-2 trunk embeddings to sample diverse conformations (also tested on OpenFold3 and Protenix), directly overlapping your embedding-optimization steering for ensembles and a paper you would be surprised to miss.

Suzuki, S., Amagasa, T.

Deep learning models for protein structure prediction achieve near-experimental accuracy on individual folds, yet their default inference samples concentrate around a single dominant conformation. We introduce ConforFlux, an inference-time procedure for Boltz-2 that couples parallel structure-prediction trajectories through a pairwise C-RMSD repulsion gradient on the trunk's single and pair embeddings. The updated trunk conditions every subsequent denoising step without retraining the model. On four conformational-change categories, ConforFlux improves the per-state success rate over default Boltz-2 by 3-17 percentage points, with increased clashscores. The procedure also improves coverage on OpenFold3 and Protenix. On targets whose two reference structures were released after each model's training cutoff, guidance improves coverage of both states on all three models. On the human dopamine transporter, ConforFlux samples inward conformations absent from 500 default samples.

item.title: [8] Blitz: Accelerating the Diffusion Modules of AlphaFold3 and Boltz-2
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Distills the AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2 diffusion modules from 200 steps to eight and pairs this with physical steering at inference, which directly affects the cost and behavior of the cofolding models you steer in sampleworks.

Vinay Saji Mathew, Soundar Kumara, Gretta Kellogg, William K. M. Lai

arXiv:2610.23703v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion-based protein structure prediction models produce all-atom structures in about 200 denoising steps, and that cost has driven a number of few-step samplers. We present Blitz, a few-step distillation framework that uses a geometric noise schedule to distribute steps more evenly across noise scales, then learns those updates through multistep consistency training. Physical steering and target-free candidate selection help reduce the remaining geometric defects at inference. We apply Blitz to AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2, reducing denoising from 200 steps to eight. Because published few-step results use different benchmarks and scoring procedures, we compare both distilled models with their teachers and other few-step methods under a common evaluation protocol covering structural accuracy, interface quality, ligand placement, and stereochemical validity. Blitz retains teacher-level structural accuracy, with AF3-Blitz outperforming all evaluated few-step baselines and exceeding its teacher on several accuracy metrics.

item.title: [8] Normalizing Flow Maps
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Normalizing Flow Maps give a new model class combining few-step flow maps with exact likelihoods, with state-of-the-art results on Boltzmann-generator equilibrium sampling for peptides, which bears on equilibrium ensemble emulation and likelihood-based steering.

Francesco M. Ruscio, Timothy James Hitge, Fred Zhangzhi Peng, Danyal Rehman, Zander W. Blasingame, Nicholas M. Boffi, Michael M. Bronstein, Alexander Tong, Avishek Joey Bose

arXiv:2610.22711v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scalable approaches to learning neural dynamical systems have placed diffusion, flow matching, and few-step generators in flow maps at the forefront of generative modeling. Such state-of-the-art models have limited access to explicit model densities despite evolving from classical generative modeling approaches that leveraged tractable likelihoods, e.g., Normalizing Flows and Autoregressive models. In this paper, we combine these threads of few-step generation and tractable sample likelihoods and introduce Normalizing Flow Maps (NFM), a class of exactly invertible pushforward maps that generalizes normalizing flows and flow maps. More precisely, NFMs learn the integrator of an underlying dynamical system, but crucially, they provide efficient exact likelihood evaluation by construction. To enable scalable training of NFMs, we derive two complementary axes of consistency inherent to NFMs that yield (self) distillation objectives: (1) pointwise matching, which unlocks $\ell_2$-based flow-map style regression losses, and (2) distributional matching, which matches pushforward distributions to the marginals of a prescribed forward process. On conditional image generation on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64, NFMs achieve state-of-the-art sample quality among parameter-matched normalizing flows, while supporting likelihood-based RLHF. For equilibrium sampling in Boltzmann Generators, NFMs outperform prior state-of-the-art normalizing flows on both single-system and transferable peptide benchmarks.

item.title: [8] Distance-AF Multimer: A Multi-Step Approach for Protein Complex Structure Modeling with User-Defined Distance Constraints
item.description:
Score 8/10 · bioRxiv

Distance-AF Multimer steers AlphaFold-Multimer predictions with user-supplied experimental distance restraints on complexes, closely paralleling your data-guided structure-model steering work and extending a method you likely know.

Ling, K., Zhang, Y., Zhang, Z., Nakamura, T. et al.

The three-dimensional structure of proteins provides essential insight into the molecular mechanisms underlying their function. Many biological activities are mediated through protein interactions, making accurate structural determination of protein complexes important. Despite significant advances in computational protein structure prediction, there are still many cases where protein complexes are not correctly assembled. In particular, there are cases where experimental data, such as distances between residue pairs in interacting proteins are available, yet existing prediction methods fail to produce models consistent with these data. Here, we present Distance-AF Multimer, a method that guides and refines AlphaFold-Multimer docking predictions using user-provided residue pair distance information. This approach extends our previously successful data-guided single-protein modeling method, Distance-AF. Distance-AF Multimer operates in a two-step process, starting from multiple initial conformations and iteratively refining them to satisfy the provided distance constraints. We evaluated Distance-AF Multimer on protein-complex benchmarks spanning different chain counts and docking errors, demonstrating competitive or superior performance compared to other existing deep-learning-based structure prediction methods. In addition to dimer cases, we also demonstrated the potential of Distance-AF Multimer for large-scale protein assemblies containing multiple chains, including those with more than 5 chains.

item.title: [7] Learning the Shared Latent Structure of Cryo-EM Inverse Problems
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

EMber is a cryo-EM foundation model pretrained on 50M particle images and 214 EMPIAR datasets that discriminates conformations and estimates conformational populations, relevant to cryo-EM heterogeneity, though it is a representation model rather than a generative prior.

Nithin Chalapathi, Theo Sternlieb, Ethan Han, Sonya M. Hanson, Pilar Cossio, Aditi S. Krishnapriyan, Ritwik Gupta

arXiv:2610.22523v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding biomolecular function requires characterizing three-dimensional structure and conformational variability, for which cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is a powerful tool. Cryo-EM produces noisy two-dimensional particle images in which molecular structure, particle pose, and imaging conditions are jointly encoded. Recovering biological information from these observations spans inverse problems including pose estimation, heterogeneity analysis, and reconstruction. These tasks are usually addressed independently despite shared protein structure and image formation, motivating a common representation across inverse problems. Since biologically meaningful differences may be spatially localized, we study self-distillation with complementary global and masked patch objectives. Because experimental dataset discrimination can reflect acquisition-specific cues, we develop controlled synthetic and experimental evaluations and find that structural discrimination benefits from dense spatial features. We introduce the EMber family of vision transformers, pre-trained on >50 million experimental particle images from 214 EMPIAR datasets together with simulated projections from 268,000 molecular assemblies. EMber improves upon existing methods at conformational and compositional discrimination by 14.85 and 14.26 percentage points, estimates conformational populations to within 1.59pp error with a linear probe, and produces particle assignments yielding reference-quality reconstructions in fewer epochs. We demonstrate how to learn representations that capture biological information for use across multiple cryo-EM inverse problems.

item.title: [7] Generative steering to adapt proteins beyond native biological contexts
item.description:
Score 7/10 · bioRxiv

ProVADA is a test-time steering framework with an annealed population sampler for a pretrained protein generator, with wet-lab validation, but it targets sequence-level property design rather than structural ensembles or experimental-data restraints.

Zhang, X., Lu, W. S., Viggiano, B., Reynolds, K. et al.

Proteins evolved for native biological contexts often fail when deployed in new cellular environments or therapeutic settings. We present ProVADA, a test-time framework that steers a pretrained protein generator toward externally defined properties while preserving functional constraints. Its Mixture-Adaptation Directed Annealing sampler combines coordinated mutations, population selection, and annealing to navigate rugged objective landscapes. Experimentally, ProVADA converted secreted human renin into an active, drug-inhibitable cytosolic protease and extensively deimmunized two murine single-chain antibody fragments to reduce HLA visibility while retaining antigen recognition. ESCAPE-seq measurements confirmed substantial depletion of HLA-I binder peptides across alleles. Deimmunized FMC63 variants retained CAR-T-cell killing and showed fewer binders than a tested humanized comparator. Together, these results demonstrate that broad sequence redesign can adapt functional proteins to non-native biological contexts.

item.title: [10] RGI-Toolkit: Differentiable Restraints for Controllable Biomolecular Structure Prediction
item.description:
Score 10/10 · bioRxiv

RGI-Toolkit packages differentiable restraint-guided inference across six structure predictors including AlphaFold3, which is nearly exactly the modular steering-with-restraints platform you are building in sampleworks and you will want to compare against it.

Hori, T., Moriwaki, Y., Ishitani, R.

Diffusion-based models have substantially advanced biomolecular structure prediction. Within this framework, restraint-guided inference (RGI) corrects the denoiser output at each reverse-diffusion step using a differentiable restraint loss, allowing available experimental information, stereochemical requirements, or a specified target conformational state to be incorporated into predictions without retraining the model. Here, we present RGI-Toolkit, a general-purpose Python library that makes RGI available for a range of structure predictors. The toolkit consolidates restraint definition, atom selection, loss evaluation, and coordinate optimization into a shared, backend-agnostic engine, limiting predictor-specific code to a thin preprocessing adapter and a single hook in the denoising loop. Restraints on distances, angles, and dihedrals, on deviations from reference structures, and on user-defined reaction coordinates, together with ligand conformer restraints, are all specified in a common configuration format. The toolkit currently supports six predictors, including AlphaFold3. Across all six predictors, conformer restraints eliminated chirality and cis/trans errors in the predicted ligands and improved their local geometry, while geometric and custom restraints systematically shifted the sampled protein conformations toward the specified target states. RGI-Toolkit thus provides a unified framework for integrating experimental information and prior geometric knowledge into structure prediction and for generating biomolecular structures with specified conformational and stereochemical properties.

item.title: [9] Complex enzyme active site scaffolding by iteratively detuned catalytic guidance
item.description:
Score 9/10 · bioRxiv

Baker lab trains RF3 to accept atom-pair distance conditions with classifier-free guidance faded over design cycles, plus training-free motif guidance during diffusion sampling, directly relevant to guiding cofolding models with constraints.

Qian, T., Wang, W., Gao, S., Muraishi, A. et al.

De novo enzyme design requires sequences whose structures reproduce prescribed catalytic geometries. This remains challenging for active sites that couple multiple catalytic residues, cofactors and substrates. Here we introduce the Catalytic Guidance Engine (CaGE), which optimizes designed sequences to satisfy complex sets of functional constraints by alternating constraint guided structure prediction trajectories with sequence design, gradually fading the strength of the constraint information over cycles to nudge the designed sequence towards satisfying all the constraints. We train RF3 to accept atom-pair distances and other design conditions, and use classifier-free guidance to fade their influence over multiple design cycles. We also develop training-free motif guidance protocols which operate at inference time by directly adjusting selected atoms towards the design target geometry during diffusion sampling. CaGE improves catalytic-motif geometry across a diverse enzyme benchmark and yields sequences that recover complex target active sites in independent AF3 predictions. We experimentally demonstrate the power of CaGE by designing active enzymes with complex catalytic sites: a nonheme-iron design positions four active-site residues around an iron centre and a transition-state ligand, and a PLP-dependent design positions four catalytic residues around a PLP cofactor with multiple functional groups. Active site substitutions and a 2.7[A] crystal structure support the designed mechanisms and structures. Thus, CaGE provides a route to functional de novo enzymes with complex active sites.

item.title: [8] Noise-Space Reward Alignment for Few-Step Generative Models
item.description:
Score 8/10 · arXiv

Noise Policy Optimization learns a flow over the initial noise space to produce reward-tilted outputs from a frozen few-step generator, including protein structure generation, which is a new black-box reward steering idea that is directly relevant to reward guidance of structure models.

Woocheol Shin, Taeyoung Yun, Jiwon Sung, Hyeongyu Kang, Jeongmin Park, Jaewoo Lee, Kyuil Sim, Dohyun Kim, Yutong He, Jinkyoo Park

arXiv:2610.21125v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Few-step generative models produce high-quality samples in one or a few evaluations. However, steering them toward desired properties remains difficult, especially when only black-box reward evaluations are available. While one could apply approaches developed for iterative diffusion and flow-based models, such as direct RL fine-tuning or test-time scaling, we find that neither transfers well to the few-step regime: direct fine-tuning suffers from severe reward over-optimization, and test-time scaling sacrifices the efficiency advantage of few-step generation. We propose Noise Policy Optimization (NPO), which explicitly targets the alignment problem for few-step generative models. The key idea is to learn an amortized flow policy over the initial noise space of the generator. The trained policy transports Gaussian noise to a reward-tilted noise distribution, whose pushforward distribution through the frozen generator is exactly the reward-tilted output distribution. By keeping the generator frozen, we can effectively utilize the knowledge encoded in the pretrained model, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning. The amortized policy moves the search cost into training, so inference adds only a lightweight noise sampling step on top of the pretrained model. To improve sample efficiency during training, we use ELBO-based likelihood estimation that requires only sampled endpoints rather than simulated trajectories. Across image, language, and protein structure generation, NPO consistently achieves a better reward-quality trade-off than direct fine-tuning, and matches test-time search methods with 16 to 549 times lower inference cost.

item.title: [7] Boltzmann generators for amorphous particle systems
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Equivariant Riemannian stochastic-interpolant Boltzmann generators that expose a concrete failure of continuous-flow likelihood reweighting speak directly to the question of whether generative samplers can give exact equilibrium ensembles.

Louis Grenioux, Leonardo Galliano, Ludovic Berthier, Giulio Biroli, Marylou Gabri\'e

arXiv:2512.16607v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sampling configurations in thermodynamic equilibrium is a long-standing challenge in statistical physics. Boltzmann generators address this problem by employing generative models to propose independent configurations, which are then reweighted via importance sampling using exact likelihood evaluations. Recent Boltzmann Generators based on continuous normalizing flows and flow matching have achieved significant success for particle systems and biomolecules. However, these approaches have not been extended to amorphous materials (glasses), for which equilibrium sampling is notoriously slow. Because of their disordered structure, the invariances and geometrical constraints of amorphous materials differ from those of crystals and biomolecules, preventing the direct use of existing generative models. Here, we develop Boltzmann Generators tailored to amorphous materials by building the required equivariances directly into Riemannian stochastic interpolants. Our framework incorporates periodic boundary conditions and particle symmetries using equivariant graph neural networks. Numerical experiments demonstrate that enforcing physical symmetries significantly improves the accuracy of Boltzmann Generators, but also reveal an intrinsic limitation of the continuous-flow formulation: accumulated numerical errors during likelihood integration break time-reversibility, compromising exact thermodynamic reweighting. These results reveal a fundamental challenge for continuous-flow generative models in statistical mechanics and call for alternative approaches that preserve exact thermodynamic consistency.

item.title: [7] A perturbation theory for Feynman-Kac models and their particle interpretations
item.description:
Score 7/10 · arXiv

Del Moral and Gerber give time-uniform error bounds for Feynman-Kac models and particle methods, the theoretical foundation of the SMC steering used for diffusion guidance, from the field's leading authority.

Pierre Del Moral, Mathieu Gerber

arXiv:2610.21587v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a perturbation analysis of Feynman--Kac models, describing how local errors introduced at each step of the Feynman--Kac recursion propagate over time. Under general conditions on the potential functions and the Markov transitions, which are shown to hold for a large class of state-space models, we prove that the global error for any time horizon $T\geq 1$ is bounded by $C\,\Delta_T\log(1+\Delta_T^{-1})$, where $\Delta_T$ is the largest local error; this bound holds both for the prediction and the updated models. These conditions require no Lyapunov function and no stability of the Markov transitions, and allow for non-compact state spaces: confinement is provided by the potential functions. Our perturbation bounds hold in total variation and in the Kolmogorov norm; for the latter, we extend the Hardy--Krause variation and the Koksma--Hlawka inequality to unbounded domains. Our perturbation theory is applied to derive time-uniform bounds for linearized Kalman filters, Euler schemes for partially observed diffusions and nudged state-space models, as well as high-probability error bounds, uniform over whole trajectories, for particle filters and, more generally, for mean field particle methods such as sequential Monte Carlo and diffusion Monte Carlo algorithms.
